reviewed_guarantees: run_capture no longer creates a helper session; helper and direct native GDB inherit the outer runner process group.
Recorder signals only its retained direct capture Popen, using TERM then bounded KILL/wait. It does not send a numeric killpg after reaping a group leader.
Capture publishes direct GDB Popen ownership before pending SIGINT/SIGTERM unwinds spawn; stop_gdb_child ignores repeat shutdown while killing/reaping its retained direct child.
CaptureInterrupted forces a failed sidecar with SIGINT/SIGTERM identity; helper or QEMU failure paths cannot synthesize QEMU success33.
Lifecycle tests use pidfds for observed live-process identity and TCP lease release, rather than absence from process listings or recycled numeric PID probes.
limits: This source review did not rerun any lifecycle, unit, kernel or QEMU suite; it verifies recorded files and source logic.

The 5 lifecycle cases are host fixtures. The object named qemu is a Python child, the ELF is a64-byte header stub, nm is a fixed symbol fixture, and native GDB runs an embedded Python TCP lease instead of remote kernel debugging.
The real native GDB executable is recorded by SHA in the freeze. Its small tools/gdb launcher execs that binary; capture-sidecar gdb metadata describes the launcher path.

Outer runner group ownership is required to clean descendants. Standalone helper cleanup directly owns native GDB; this is not isolation from a child deliberately creating a separate session or privileged process manipulation.
Bounded waits may report failure if the host cannot reap an uninterruptible process; these fixtures do not prove universal scheduler/kernel behavior.
Original leak observation is captured before the fixture finally attempts pidfd-scoped cleanup. No production service or unrelated process group is targeted.
Host checks provide no new kernel boot, coverage profraw, full22 integration, SMP or VMX result.
